text: The console only reads. A query starts with SELECT. Nothing here can change the evidence.
note: The console reads, never writes. A player who typed DELETE or UPDATE is not making a mistake so much as asking for something the game does not do, and the sentence says so without scolding.

text: More than 1,000,000 rows. Each table after FROM multiplies the rows by its own count. Link the tables with JOIN … ON, or add a WHERE.
note: A result too large to hold: every table listed in FROM multiplies the rows by its own count, and five copies of a 52-row table is 380 million. `sqlEngine` stops at a million and throws a marker; this is what the player reads.

text: {table} is sealed. Clear checkpoint {number}, {title}, and it is yours.
note: A table the case holds but the player has not earned. SQLite calls it "no such table", which is indistinguishable from a typo, and the schema panel is listing the name by which the player found it. `{number}` is the checkpoint that opens it and `{title}` is that checkpoint's own title.

text: {table} is sealed. You have not requisitioned it yet.
note: group diagnosis: What SQLite said, in the player's terms.

text: This bracket closes one that was never opened.
This bracket is never closed. Every ( needs a ).
This text never closes. A value in quotes needs one at each end: 'Fire'.
The semicolon ends the query. Everything after it is a second query, and the console runs one at a time.
{keyword} and {rest} need a space between them. As one word it reads as a name, and there is nothing by that name.
note: Two halves of one word the player typed without a space — `SELECTcity`.

text: A space is missing between {left} and {right}. SQLite reads it anyway and answers, so nothing looks wrong.
note: A closing quote run straight into the next word — `'2026-03-02'AND`. SQLite accepts it and answers, which is why this one is worth a sentence: the player is not told the query failed, they are handed rows.

text: 2 commas in a row. There is nothing between them.
A comma with nothing after it. A list separates its items. It does not end with a separator.
{clause} belongs before {after}, and here it comes after. The order is fixed: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
note: `{clause}` is a SQL keyword — WHERE, GROUP BY — and the list after it is the order itself, so neither is translated.

text: There is nothing between those quotes, so nothing can match. Put the value inside them.
note: Two quotes with nothing between them. It compiles, it runs and it returns nothing, so the desk said "no rows matched" and the player read that as an answer about the data. Fourteen Russian sessions submitted one on the same checkpoint: the identifiers are typed in Latin and the values are Cyrillic, so a filter costs a keyboard layout switch in the middle of the line, and a switch that does not ta…

text: Nothing is ever equal to NULL, not even NULL. The test is always false. Say IS NULL instead.
BETWEEN takes its 2 ends joined by AND, with no brackets and no comma. Write {fix}.
note: `BETWEEN ('17:31', '17:38')`, the two ends written as a list. `{fix}` is the same query rebuilt from the player's own two values, `BETWEEN '17:31' AND '17:38'`, and is SQL: never translated.

text: There is no column called {token}. Did you mean {near}? If {token} is a value, it needs quotes: '{token}'.
note: Two forms of the same fault: with a column close enough to suggest, and without. The suggestion is only offered when it can be proved.

text: {token} has no quotes, so SQL reads it as a column name. A text value needs them: '{token}'.
Without quotes, SQL reads {token} as a subtraction and compares with {result}. A date needs quotes. Did you mean '{token}'?
note: A date or a time typed with no quotes. `{token}` is what the player typed, `{result}` what SQL computed from it: the subtraction is the whole explanation, so it is printed rather than described.

text: Without quotes, SQL cannot read the colon in {token}. A time needs quotes. Did you mean '{token}'?
IN wants its list in brackets: IN ('one', 'two').
LIKE with no % has to match the whole value. Put % where the rest of the text may be: '%fire%'.
{token} on its own is not a test. Name the column again: {clause} column = {token}.
note: `{clause}` is WHERE or HAVING, and `column` in the example is the word the player should replace — a placeholder, not a column of any table.

text: Double quotes mean a column name, and there is no column called {inner}. Text values take single quotes: '{inner}'.
A comma is missing before {token}. Without one, SQL reads it as a nickname for {prev} and returns a single column.
note: The commonest fault in the game, and the reason `nickname` is the word: an alias is what SQL calls it, and a beginner does not know the word yet.

text: A comma is missing before {token}. A name and a function cannot sit side by side. SQL stops at the bracket and refuses the whole query.
A comma is missing before {token}, and there is no column called {token}. Did you mean {prev}, {near}?
note: The missing comma with a misspelling on top of it, which is why it names three words: what was typed, what it was typed after, and the column it is one keystroke from. Without the comma the query runs and returns one column, so nothing else in the game will mention it.

text: WHERE chooses the rows, and {fn} counts the rows WHERE chose, so there is nothing there yet. Filter a total in HAVING, after the GROUP BY.
note: WHERE and HAVING are keywords and stay as they are. `{fn}` arrives upper-cased, the way the player has to type it.

text: {alias} is the name given in the SELECT, and WHERE is read first, so the name does not exist yet. Write the column out again here, or filter it in HAVING.
{token} is a column of {other}, and this query only reads {table}. Requisition {other} and join it, or read the column from there.
note: `{table}` is what the FROM reads, `{other}` the table that has the column. Both are identifiers the player types.

text: 2 tables with nothing between them. {token} is being read as a nickname for {prev}. A JOIN needs the word JOIN and an ON.
Counting collapses every row into one, so only one {column} can come back, and SQL picks it at random. Add GROUP BY {column} to count per {column}.
{column} is not in the GROUP BY, so each group shows whichever {column} SQL happened to read last. Group by it too, or leave it out.
HAVING filters groups, and without a GROUP BY there is only one group. To filter rows, use WHERE.
There is no table to read from here. Add FROM and the table name.
{table} is already in the FROM, so this joins it to itself. Join the other table: FROM {other} JOIN {table} ON …
note: The same table on both sides of a JOIN, with no nickname to tell them apart. `{table}` is what the player typed; `{other}` the case's other table. Schema names, never translated.

text: {table} is already in the FROM, so this joins it to itself. Join the other table instead.
This JOIN has no matching columns, so it pairs every row with every row. Add ON table_a.column = table_b.column.
Nothing in this query is called {prefix}. Did you mean {near}?
Nothing in this query is called {prefix}. A prefix has to be a table in the FROM, or a nickname given to one.
LIMIT takes the first rows, and with no ORDER BY it is SQL's choice which those are. Sort first to take the biggest, or the earliest.
